w: Its bell tower collapsed in 1405, was rebuilt, then crowned in 1859 with a gilded Virgin Mary visible across the city. Inside sits the Gothic mausoleum of Pope John XXII, shuffled around, damaged in the Revolution, and finally put back in 1840 -- the same year the cathedral became a monument historique.
s: A gilded Virgin over the popes' old palace
_facts: Romanesque cathedral built mainly in the second half of the 12th century, next to the Palais des Papes
bell tower collapsed 1405, rebuilt 1425; gilded statue of the Virgin Mary added atop it in 1859
contains the 14th-century Gothic mausoleum of Pope John XXII; monument historique since 1840, part of the 1995 UNESCO listing

w: Built in the 14th century as the bishops of Avignon's own residence, this palace on the square facing the Papal Palace now holds early Renaissance "primitives" -- paintings once reclaimed from the Louvre, plus works of the Avignon school. Opened in 1976, and folded into the city's UNESCO listing in 1995.
s: Renaissance primitives in the bishops' old home
_facts: 14th-century building, originally residence of the bishops of Avignon, on the square facing the Palais des Papes
houses early Renaissance 'primitive' paintings, including the Giampietro Campana collection reclaimed from the Louvre, and Avignon school works
opened 1976; made part of the Avignon UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995

w: Avignon's main museum has lived in two places since the 1980s -- fine art in an 18th-century townhouse, ancient stone in a former Jesuit chapel down the road. Between them: goldwork, faience, tapestries, and ethnographic collections reaching as far as Oceania and Africa.
s: Avignon's flagship museum, split in two buildings
_facts: the main museum in Avignon, run by the Fondation Calvet
since the 1980s split between an 18th-century hotel particulier for fine arts and a separate Lapidary Museum
collections include goldwork, faience, porcelain, tapestries, ironwork, archaeology, and Asian, Oceanic and African ethnography

w: Jacques Doucet, the Parisian couturier, built a private art collection that eventually passed to his widow's heirs -- and in 1996, per their wishes, it became this museum inside an 18th-century townhouse on rue Laboureur. Two centuries of paintings, still under one roof.
s: A couturier's private art collection, made public
_facts: museum at 5 rue Laboureur, in the 18th-century hotel de Massilian
established 1996 following the wishes of Jean and Paulette Angladon-Dubrujeaud, heirs of couturier Jacques Doucet's widow
collection spans artworks from the 18th to 20th century

w: A 17th-century Jesuit chapel, begun in 1616, now shelters the Calvet Museum's classical stonework -- Greek, Etruscan, Roman and Gallo-Roman sculpture packed under a vaulted ceiling built for prayer, not archaeology. Listed as a monument historique since 1928.
s: Ancient stone stored inside a Jesuit chapel
_facts: lapidarium-museum housing the Calvet Museum's Greek, Etruscan, Roman and Gallo-Roman sculpture since the 1980s
based at 27 rue de la Republique in a 17th-century building, the former chapel of the city's Jesuit college, begun 1616
designated monument historique on 21 June 1928

w: Named for Esprit Requien, the Avignon-born naturalist who died on Corsica in 1851, this natural history museum keeps some of entomologist Jean-Henri Fabre's work on display -- insects and specimens standing in for a life spent cataloguing the region's wild things.
s: A natural history museum named for a local naturalist
_facts: natural history museum in Avignon
displays some of Jean-Henri Fabre's work
named after naturalist Esprit Requien (1788, Avignon - 1851, Bonifacio)

w: Raised in the first half of the 14th century in Villeneuve-les-Avignon, this fortress once stood as the Kingdom of France's stronghold facing Papal territory across the Rhone -- two powers, one river between them, and this the watchtower on the French side.
s: France's watchtower facing the popes' Avignon
_facts: medieval fortress in the commune of Villeneuve-les-Avignon, Gard
dates from the first half of the 14th century
Villeneuve-les-Avignon sat on the French side of the Rhone opposite Papal-held Avignon

w: For nearly seven centuries, from the 11th to the 18th, this abbey was home to canons regular and served as the mother house of the entire Order of Saint-Ruf. Its founding glory didn't last forever -- by 1158 it had already been demoted to a mere priory.
s: Mother house of a medieval canonical order
_facts: house of canons regular in Avignon between the 11th and 18th centuries
was the mother house and original headquarters of the Order of Saint-Ruf
reduced to a priory after 1158

w: The first opera house here opened in 1825 and burned to the ground just twenty-one years later. Architects Leon Feuchere and Theodore Charpentier rebuilt it within the year, and that second building -- a monument historique since 1988 -- is still staging shows two centuries on.
s: An opera house rebuilt from its own ashes
_facts: opera house first built 1824-1825, opened 30 October 1825
destroyed by fire on 26 January 1846; rebuilt 1846-1847 by architects Leon Feuchere and Theodore Charpentier
designated monument historique in 1988

w: This tower marked the French end of the Saint-Benezet Bridge -- the one from the song -- linking France to Papal Avignon across the Rhone. Built by 1302 over local protests, a third storey added later, it outlived the bridge: when the crossing was abandoned in 1669, the tower alone was spared demolition in 1822.
s: Where the famous Pont d'Avignon met dry land
_facts: medieval tower marking the French terminus of the Saint-Benezet Bridge (Pont d'Avignon) across the Rhone
built for King Philippe-le-Bel, two-storey tower completed 1302 despite local protests; third storey added mid-14th century
bridge abandoned 1669; town demolished the rest of the fortress in 1822 but kept the tower, listed monument historique in 1862
